newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh T-bill yields show falling inflation-c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh T-bill yields show falling inflation-c.bank.

text.p: Falling yields on Kazakh treasury bills indicate inflation may be lower than expected this year, the head of the central bank said on Thursday.
National Bank governor Uraz Dzhandosov said falling inflation and yields would probably allow the central bank to cut its key interest rates on Friday.

"Banks and investors, who are mostly foreign ones, are now confident that the National Bank will manage to achieve its inflation targets, and yields on MKM bills reflect lower inflation," Dzhandosov told a news conference.

"With a probability of 90 percent, we will take a decision on new cuts of our basic rates. This trend reflects the fall of yields on the government securities market," Dzhandosov said of Friday's meeting of the bank's administrative council.

The yield on three-month T-bills fell to a low of 14.59 percent at an auction on Tuesday from 17.23 percent on May 13. The yield on six-month paper fell to 19.90 percent on May 12 from 22.97 percent on April 28. Twelve-month bills fell to 22.59 percent on May 5 from 26.17 percent on April 7.

Dzhandosov said inflation was firmly under control and consumer prices grew by 5.5 percent in the first four months of the year. "This is in line with our expectations, and inflation this year may fall below our target of 17 percent."
On May 1 the National Bank cut its annual refinancing rate to 30 percent from 35 percent, Lombard rate to 28 percent from 30 percent and overnight rate to 23 percent from 25 percent.

Dzhandosov declined to make forecasts of T-bill yields at future auctions but said: "I do not think the lowest psychological barrier has been passed. Yields reasonably reflect future inflation and are still profitable for investors."

Kazakh bankers have previously said that the government and the National Bank were interested in attracting foreign investors and cutting T-bill yields to force local banks to boost long-term investment in the economy.
"This is only one of many factors," Dzhandosov said.

He said another positive effect of low inflation and the stable tenge currency was that the population would believe in stability and "take their savings from under their mattresses to put in local banks".
He declined to say how much money people were saving and said the banks were likely to channel this money to the rebounding economy.
"The current stabilisation of output needs loans to transform into steady economic growth," he said.
The Kazakh government expects gross domestic product to grow by 1.5 percent this year.
